title: MZ Trying to load data from URL

posts.author: echocondria
ShadowDragon
caethyril
posts.body:
I imagine you've tested with an event like this?
◆Text：None, None, Window, Bottom
：    ：Hi! I'm about to fetch some data!
◆Plugin Command：FetchExample, Fetch Data
：              ：URL = https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1
◆Text：None, None, Window, Bottom
：    ：Hey, did it work?
In that case, if you've named the plugin file
FetchExample.js
(to match the registration in the code) then the command will run as intended.
However, fetch runs asynchronously, and the interpreter moves immediately to the next command (Show Text), so the
$gameMessage.add
call in your plugin will not display like you want it to. If you removed the "Hey, did it work?" message (and didn't activate any other event in the meantime) then this example would work as you expect.
Spoiler:
technical explanation
The message window (Show Text) only displays one message at a time. The text to display is determined when the message "starts" (see the
startMessage
method of
Window_Message
in rmmz_windows.js); any additions during the message will technically be added to
$gameMessage
, but that won't affect the message being displayed.
The message is cleared when the window ends the current message (see the
terminateMessage
method, ibid). This means that if your fetch operation completes while another message is showing, your addition is effectively ignored.
A low-quality, unreliable workaround would be to simply add a command like Wait 30 frames after the command. It's a bad idea because you can't be sure that it will work correctly in edge cases.
I recommend you use something to let the interpreter know when to proceed. You could add a
finally
clause to your plugin command code for something like that. E.g.
Implement a new wait mode:
Add a patch for the
updateWaitMode
method of
Game_Interpreter
, for your new wait mode.
Use
this.setWaitMode("yourWaitModeName")
before the
fetch
starts.
Make whatever change necessary in the
finally
clause to end your new wait mode.
Note that arrow functions do not have a
this
value, so you'll also need to write your plugin command as a full
function(args) { ... }
for this approach to work. Plugin commands run in the context of the calling interpreter.
Alternatively, turn a switch on (or off): you could then use the Loop, Branch, and Break Loop commands immediately after the plugin command to prevent further progress until that switch is toggled. That would be a somewhat clunky solution, but doesn't require any special knowledge to implement or customise.

posts.author: caethyril
posts.body:
echocondria said:
I'm having an issue with the plugin command even firing at all. I changed it to just log to the console and that doesn't ever show up.
Click to expand...
Before posting my previous reply, I tested your code, as-is, and it worked as I described. I've attached the file so you can try it for yourself~
I guess the problem is related to this:
caethyril said:
if you've named the plugin file
FetchExample.js
(to match the registration in the code)
Click to expand...
I.e. you may have saved the plugin with a different filename. Note that filenames are case-sensitive here, e.g.
fetchExample.js
and
FetchExample.js
are different files. The command uses the filename: if that doesn't match a registered function then the command will be skipped.
In case it helps: you can enter
PluginManager._commands
into the console to see all registered plugin commands.
